title: Building a linked structure
lesson:
Time to build a data structure that owns memory, using everything so far. A **singly linked list** is a chain of **nodes**. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; the last node's `next` is empty.

```
head -> [ "jump" ] -> [ "move" ] -> [ "build" ] -> (nothing)
```

Who owns the nodes? The list owns the first node, and **each node owns the next one**. That is a perfect fit for `unique_ptr`:

```
struct Node
{
    std::string action;
    std::unique_ptr<Node> next;   // owns the rest of the chain
};

std::unique_ptr<Node> head;       // the list owns the first node
```

**Push to the front** (O(1), no matter how long the list is):

```
auto n = std::make_unique<Node>("jump");
n->next = std::move(head);   // the new node takes over the old chain
head = std::move(n);         // the list now owns the new node
```

**Pop from the front:**

```
std::string a = head->action;
head = std::move(head->next);   // the old head is deleted automatically
```

**Walking the list** uses plain non-owning pointers, since you are only looking:

```
for (const Node* n = head.get(); n; n = n->next.get())
    std::cout << n->action << "\n";
```

A list where you only push and pop at the front is a **stack** (last in, first out): an undo history, a pathfinding backtrack, a stack of open menus. Add a raw `Node* tail` pointing at the last node and push at the back while popping at the front, and you have a **queue** (first in, first out): patients waiting at a clinic, orders waiting for a robot arm, enemies waiting to spawn. The tail pointer doesn't own anything; it just remembers where the end is. When the queue empties, set it back to `nullptr`.

**Removing from the middle** is neat with a pointer to the link you are standing on:

```
std::unique_ptr<Node>* link = &head;
while (*link && (*link)->action != target) link = &(*link)->next;
if (*link) *link = std::move((*link)->next);   // unlink and delete
```

**Clean destruction.** When the list is destroyed, `head` deletes node 1, which deletes node 2, and so on: no leaks, no destructor needed. One catch: that chain is a recursion, and a list of a million nodes can overflow the stack. Long-lived lists give themselves a simple loop destructor: `while (head) head = std::move(head->next);`.

In real game code you'll use `std::vector`, `std::deque` and Unreal's `TArray`/`TQueue` much more than hand-made lists. Building one yourself is how you learn ownership properly, and the same node-and-link idea is behind trees, scene graphs and behaviour trees.

notes: Each node owns the next through a unique_ptr, and head owns the first node.
Pushing to the front moves the old chain into the new node, then moves the new node into head.
The walk uses .get(): plain pointers for looking, because the loop doesn't own anything.
head = std::move(head->next) pops: the old head is deleted when head is reassigned.

exercises.title: Undo stack
exercises.prompt:
Write class UndoStack, a stack of action names built from Nodes linked by unique_ptr (Node is given):
- void push(const std::string& action) puts an action on top.
- std::string pop() removes and returns the top action, or "" if the stack is empty.
- std::string peek() const returns the top action without removing it, or "".
- int size() const and bool empty() const.
Popped nodes must be deleted, and destroying the stack must delete every node.

tests.call: []{ UndoStack s; s.push("move"); s.push("jump"); return s.peek() + "," + std::to_string(s.size()); }()
[]{ UndoStack s; s.push("build"); s.push("move"); s.push("jump"); std::string a = s.pop(); std::string b = s.pop(); return a + "," + b + "," + std::to_string(s.size()); }()
[]{ UndoStack s; s.push("x"); s.pop(); return std::to_string(s.empty()) + s.pop() + s.peek(); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Popping or peeking an empty stack returns "" and must not crash.

tests.call: []{ int before = Node::alive; UndoStack s; s.push("a"); s.push("b"); s.push("c"); s.pop(); return Node::alive - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: The popped node must be deleted: head = std::move(head->next);

tests.call: []{ int before = Node::alive; { UndoStack s; for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) s.push("step"); } return Node::alive - before; }()

hints: push: auto n = std::make_unique<Node>(action); n->next = std::move(head); head = std::move(n); count++;
pop: if (!head) return ""; std::string a = head->action; head = std::move(head->next); count--; return a;
A loop destructor is a nice touch: ~UndoStack() { while (head) head = std::move(head->next); }

exercises.title: Clinic queue
exercises.prompt:
Write class PatientQueue, a first-in-first-out queue of names built from QNodes (given). Keep std::unique_ptr<QNode> head (the front, which owns the chain) and a plain QNode* tail (the back, not owning).
- void join(const std::string& name) adds a patient at the back.
- std::string next() removes and returns the patient at the front, or "" if nobody is waiting.
- std::string front() const returns the front name without removing it, or "".
- int size() const.
The queue must keep working after it has been emptied, and served patients' nodes must be deleted.

tests.call: []{ PatientQueue q; q.join("Amina"); q.join("Juma"); q.join("Otieno"); return q.front() + "," + std::to_string(q.size()); }()
[]{ PatientQueue q; q.join("Amina"); q.join("Juma"); q.join("Otieno"); std::string a = q.next(); std::string b = q.next(); return a + "," + b + "," + q.front(); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: First in, first out: join at the tail, serve from the head.

tests.call: []{ PatientQueue q; q.join("Amina"); q.next(); std::string a = q.next(); return a + "|" + q.front() + "|" + std::to_string(q.size()); }()
[]{ PatientQueue q; q.join("Amina"); q.join("Juma"); q.next(); q.next(); q.join("Wanjiru"); q.join("Otieno"); std::string a = q.next(); std::string b = q.next(); return a + "," + b; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: When the queue becomes empty, set tail back to nullptr, and when joining an empty queue the new node is both head and tail.

tests.call: []{ int before = QNode::alive; PatientQueue q; q.join("a"); q.join("b"); q.join("c"); q.next(); return QNode::alive - before; }()
[]{ int before = QNode::alive; { PatientQueue q; q.join("a"); q.join("b"); } return QNode::alive - before; }()

hints: join: auto n = std::make_unique<QNode>(name); QNode* raw = n.get(); if (tail) tail->next = std::move(n); else head = std::move(n); tail = raw; count++;
Take raw = n.get() BEFORE moving n, because after the move n is empty.
next: if (!head) return ""; read the name; head = std::move(head->next); if (!head) tail = nullptr; count--;

exercises.title: Find and remove waypoints

tests.call: []{ Route r; r.pushFront("well"); r.pushFront("farm"); r.pushFront("gate"); return std::to_string(r.contains("farm")) + std::to_string(r.indexOf("well")) + std::to_string(r.indexOf("cave")); }()
[]{ Route r; r.pushFront("well"); r.pushFront("farm"); r.pushFront("gate"); bool ok = r.remove("farm"); return std::to_string(ok) + " " + r.list() + " " + std::to_string(r.size()); }()
[]{ Route r; r.pushFront("well"); r.pushFront("farm"); r.pushFront("gate"); r.remove("gate"); r.remove("well"); return r.list(); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Removing the first one means changing head itself; removing the last one means changing the previous node's next.

tests.call: []{ Route r; r.pushFront("well"); return std::to_string(r.remove("cave")) + std::to_string(r.size()); }()
[]{ Route r; return std::to_string(r.remove("x")) + std::to_string(r.contains("x")) + std::to_string(r.indexOf("x")); }()
[]{ Route r; r.pushFront("a"); r.pushFront("b"); r.pushFront("a"); r.remove("a"); return r.list(); }()
[]{ int before = Waypoint::alive; Route r; r.pushFront("a"); r.pushFront("b"); r.remove("a"); return Waypoint::alive - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: Removing must delete the waypoint: move its next into the link that owned it.

hints: contains can just be: return indexOf(name) != -1;
indexOf: walk with const Waypoint* w = head.get() and a counter.
remove: std::unique_ptr<Waypoint>* link = &head; while (*link) { if ((*link)->name == name) { *link = std::move((*link)->next); count--; return true; } link = &(*link)->next; } return false;

quiz.q: In a unique_ptr linked list, who owns node 3?
quiz.why: Each node owns the next one; the list owns only the head.

choices: Pops the front node, which gets deleted
quiz.why: The old head loses its owner and is deleted.

quiz.q: Why is a queue's tail a plain pointer, not a unique_ptr?
choices: The node is already owned by the node before it; two unique_ptrs can't own one node
unique_ptr can't point at the end
quiz.why: The tail only remembers where the end is; it doesn't own.

quiz.q: Which is a stack (last in, first out)?
quiz.why: Undo takes the most recent action first.

quiz.q: A queue is emptied by next(). What must happen to tail?
choices: Set it to nullptr, or it dangles at a deleted node
quiz.why: The node it pointed at was deleted.

cards.a: struct Node { T value; std::unique_ptr<Node> next; };
for (const Node* n = head.get(); n; n = n->next.get())
Stack: last in, first out. Queue: first in, first out.

explain: Explain how a linked list built from unique_ptrs cleans itself up, and why a queue's tail pointer must not own its node.
